forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Hampshire fire authority defers £10.2m of capital spending and cuts reserve payments by £4.2m to bridge 2027/28 gap
news_drafts.lead:
Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority is deferring £10.223m of capital spending (money spent on things that last, such as buildings and vehicles) from 2026/27 and reducing its contributions to reserves (money set aside) by £4.163m in 2027/28, rather than setting a savings target for that year. An update report to the authority's meeting on 8 October sets out the approach.

The authority's medium-term financial plan, agreed in February 2026, identified a budget gap from 2026/27 onwards. The report attributes it to inflation, pressures in delivering services and a £2.9m reduction in settlement funding (the government's grant) over the three-year settlement covering 2026/27 to 2028/29.

The authority is working on five strands. Strand A is reprioritising spending and deferring capital work. Strand B is a temporary cut in reserve contributions. Strand C is a review of how the service operates, under a programme called Ambition 2030. Strand D is a request for extra flexibility over council tax, and Strand E is continued lobbying for government funding. The paper describes A and B as short-term solutions while longer-term options are developed. It says: "All else being equal, the mitigations in Strand A and B will not result in the budget gap being closed on a sustainable basis and the work under Strand C will therefore be important in presenting options for longer term financial sustainability."

news_drafts.headline: Hampshire Pension Fund facing £70m annual cash shortfall from next year as investments transfer to external manager
news_drafts.lead: Hampshire's pension fund will need investment income of £140m annually from 2026/27 to cover the £70m gap between pension contributions received and benefits paid, according to the Pension Fund Panel and Board meeting on 25 September. The fund, managing £11.2bn of assets, will depend on achieving its long-term return target of 5.9% to bridge this deficit while maintaining a £60m operational cash buffer. From 1 April this year, investment management transferred to LGPS Central, a Financial Conduct Authority-regulated pool serving 14 councils including Hampshire. The fund operates on an 80% probability of meeting its funding objectives, meaning a 1 in 5 chance of falling below its 70% minimum funding level in the worst economic scenarios. Officers highlighted that the real estate portfolio remains £243m short of its target allocation, a gap likely to widen as the fund grows, and flagged that private equity and infrastructure mandates are missing three-year performance targets, though longer-term results show both outperforming over five years.

news_drafts.headline: Hampshire internal audit 14 per cent complete as of late July; audit found 642 care packages without required monitoring
news_drafts.lead: Hampshire's internal audit plan is severely behind schedule, with only 14 per cent completed against a 90 per cent target as of late July. The Audit Committee heard that none of the audits delivered to draft stage have met agreed timescales, and only a third reached final stage on time. The shortfall has real consequences: an audit found 642 care packages went without required weekly monitoring checks over seven weeks, with five providers failing to submit variations for 80 per cent or more of their packages. The council's external auditor also identified a risk of significant weakness in the council's financial sustainability and said full assurance over property valuations will not be restored until 2027/28, pushing an unqualified audit opinion to 2029/30 at the earliest.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Capital Payments Reserve of £47.7m to be fully drawn to finance capital programme
findings.detail: The authority's Capital Payments Reserve is being consumed to finance capital investment, with £24.5m already spent in previous years and £23.2m more scheduled across 2026/27 to 2030/31, depleting the reserve entirely by the end of the programme period.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the authority is prudently managing cash reserves and will retain sufficient liquidity for future flexibility and contingencies.
findings.figures: Capital Payments Reserve £47,691k total; previous years' spend £24,462k; scheduled future draws of £5,406k (2026/27), £8,869k (2027/28), £436k (2028/29), £5,440k (2029/30), £3,078k (2030/31)

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast significantly below February estimate (£13.7m vs £22.7m) and external debt remains well below budget; Authority within prudential borrowing limits.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure for 2026/27 is forecast at £13.7m compared to the February 2026 estimate of £22.7m, reflecting deferral of planned fire station rebuilds and vehicle acquisitions. External debt at 30 June 2026 was £26.4m, significantly below the forecast of £34.3m. Financing costs are 2.4% of net revenue stream (February forecast: 2.8%). The Authority remains within authorised borrowing limits (actual £27.4m against limit of £53.3m).
findings.matters: Significant reduction in capital investment signals constrained investment capacity. While current debt metrics are healthy, potential future borrowing to fund deferred capital expenditure could place ongoing revenue pressure on the budget.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2026/27: £13.7m forecast (vs £22.7m February estimate); external debt 30 June 2026: £26.4m (vs £34.3m forecast); financing costs 2.4% of net revenue stream; borrowing headroom £25.9m against authorised limit
findings.quote: The Authority has remained within the authorised limit for the maximum affordable amount of external debt and has ensured that over the medium term debt will only be for capital purposes.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: £1.126m in delivery pressures approved for 2027/28 including conversion of fixed-term firefighter contracts to permanent posts and specialist capabilities expansion.
findings.detail: The Authority has approved three delivery pressures for budget inclusion: £435k for replacing fixed-term firefighter contracts with permanent posts (to mitigate unfair dismissal risk from January 2027 legislation changes), £380k for increased operational officer establishment to address flexibility and resilience gaps, and £311k for specialist capabilities including Urban Search and Rescue compliance following national resilience audits in 2025. These are in addition to other forecast pressures totalling £1.614m, including an indicative £1.2m for Service Delivery capacity to support Safety Plan objectives. Any 2026/27 costs will be offset by vacancies or contingency.
findings.matters: Significant establishment growth at a time of budget pressure indicates the service believes statutory and operational requirements cannot be met within current staffing and capability levels, adding to structural cost pressures.
findings.figures: Approved pressures: £435k permanent firefighter posts, £380k operational officer establishment, £311k specialist capabilities; total approved £1.126m; other identified pressures £1.614m including £1.2m indicative for Service Delivery capacity
findings.quote: The Chief Fire Officer has identified a need to increase capacity within Service Delivery to ensure the Authority can meet statutory and national requirements and to support resilience and succession planning.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Authority's council tax precept is below average for fire and rescue sector and below government settlement formula assumption; seeking additional flexibility from government for above-referendum-threshold increase.
findings.detail: The Authority's council tax precept is lower than the notional average assumed in the government settlement formula and below most other fire and rescue authorities in England. The settlement allows a maximum £5 per year increase for Band D without triggering a referendum. The Authority is being instructed to contact MHCLG to request additional council tax flexibility to allow a higher increase without triggering a referendum. Northamptonshire Commissioner Fire and Rescue Authority was granted permission for a £10 increase for 2026/27. Each £1 increase in council tax generates approximately £0.8m in revenue.
findings.matters: Growing dependency on council tax increases to close a structural budget gap, combined with below-average current precept, suggests the Authority expects limited central government funding solutions and may face local taxpayer resistance to above-settlement increases.
findings.figures: £5 maximum increase without referendum (settlement assumption); each £1 increase generates approximately £0.8m; Northamptonshire granted £10 increase; Authority precept below notional formula assumption and below peer average
findings.quote: The Authority's actual council tax is lower than the notional average and it is not possible to meet the average the Authority is assumed to be able to generate without setting an above referendum limit council tax increase.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Revenue contributions to reserves will be reduced by £4.163m in 2027/28; general reserve currently below peer average for fire authorities but strategy to rebuild underway.
findings.detail: The Authority plans to reduce annual revenue contributions to reserves from 2027/28 in response to the budget gap: ICT reserve contribution reduced by £368k, capital payments reserve by £3.5m, and transformation reserve by £275k, with planned reinstatement beginning 2029/30. The Chief Financial Officer noted in February 2026 that the Authority holds a 'relatively low general reserve balance in percentage terms when compared with other fire and rescue authorities' and recommended increasing the general reserve to approximately 5% of annual revenue budget. The proposed approach includes transferring excess 2026/27 interest income and capital financing savings to general reserve and bringing forward a planned £2.5m reallocation from the Budget Equalisation Reserve.
findings.matters: Reducing revenue contributions to reserves to manage a structural budget gap is a sign of financial pressure and limits the Authority's financial flexibility for unexpected demands. Low general reserves relative to peers constrains emergency response capacity and increases vulnerability to further demand or funding shocks.
findings.figures: Reserve contribution reductions: ICT £368k, capital payments £3.5m, transformation £275k; total 2027/28 reduction £4.163m; target general reserve ~5% of annual revenue budget; planned £2.5m reallocation from Budget Equalisation Reserve to general reserve in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Chief Financial Officer noted that the Authority held a relatively low general reserve balance in percentage terms when compared with other fire and rescue authorities, but that this was mitigated by relatively large earmarked reserves.
